blocks.content: Once you know the individual pieces (client, daemon, images, registry), it helps to see them assembled into the loop a team actually runs, day to day, from writing a Dockerfile to a container running in production.

The full path from code to a running container follows the same five steps almost every time: write a Dockerfile describing the environment, build an image from it, tag that image with a version, push it to a registry, and finally pull and run it wherever it needs to live.

blocks.alt: The same five steps, every time

docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

docker run -d myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

blocks.content: Day to day, most of your time is spent in a much smaller loop: edit code, rebuild the image, run it locally, check the result, and repeat. Tools like bind mounts and Docker Compose (covered in later modules) exist specifically to make this inner loop faster by avoiding a full rebuild for every tiny change.

blocks.alt: The tight loop you live in most of the day

blocks.content: 3. How a Team Shares One Image
blocks.text: 3. How a Team Shares One Image

blocks.content: A registry is what turns an individual's local workflow into a team workflow. One developer (or CI) builds and pushes an image once, and every teammate, and every environment, pulls that identical image rather than each rebuilding it themselves from source.

blocks.alt: Build once, everyone else just pulls

blocks.content: 4. The Same Image, Promoted Through Environments
blocks.text: 4. The Same Image, Promoted Through Environments

blocks.content: The healthiest version of this workflow builds an image exactly once and promotes that same artifact through dev, staging, and production, rather than rebuilding at each stage. This is the concrete mechanism behind the "consistency" benefit Docker is known for: nothing gets rebuilt on the way to production, so nothing can drift on the way there either.

blocks.alt: One build, promoted unchanged through every environment

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: The full Docker workflow is Dockerfile to image to tag to push to pull to run, the same shape whether it is one developer or an entire team.
Promoting the exact same built image through dev, staging, and production (never rebuilding along the way) is what actually delivers on Docker's "consistency" promise.
